title: Idaho Parachuted 76 Beavers Out of Planes. On Purpose. #shorts

authoring.run: scheduled short run, 20 Nov 2026; first slate idea (case 042)

description:
Case 042. In 1948 beavers around the lake town of McCall, Idaho, were felling trees and building dams that flooded yards as more people built homes there, so Idaho Fish and Game set out to move them deep into the backcountry of the Chamberlain Basin, in what is now the Frank Church-River of No Return Wilderness. There were no roads, and carrying beavers in by horse and mule went badly: in the words of Fish and Game's Elmo Heter, "Horses and mules become spooky and quarrelsome when loaded with a struggling, odorous pair of live beavers." Heter's answer was war-surplus parachutes and a wooden box that held together in the air and sprang open when it landed. An old male beaver the crew called Geronimo was the test pilot: dropped on a landing field again and again, until he crawled back into his box on his own, ready to go again. That year 76 beavers were parachuted into the backcountry, Geronimo among the first, with three young females; 75 of them landed safely. When Fish and Game checked the next year, the beavers had built dams and lodges and were on their way to new colonies, Geronimo's among them. Rook didn't believe it either.

Animated reconstruction of a true story. The plane, the boxes, the town, the corral, the field and everyone in them are generic low-poly shapes with no makes, markings or logos, and nobody's likeness is attempted. Staging details such as the look of the box, where the mule was loaded and the people around Heter are illustrative. Narrated with a synthetic voice (Kokoro).

Sources: Boise State Public Radio (2015); Wikipedia, 'Beaver drop'; Smithsonian Magazine (Smart News); National Geographic (2021); Post Register via HeraldNet (2014); Idaho Statesman via East Idaho News (2023); Smithsonian Air & Space, 'Beavers On Parachutes' (on Heter's 1950 paper 'Transplanting Beavers by Airplane and Parachute').

source_notes: Read for this run on 20 Nov 2026 through a fetch tool, all seven pages loaded: Boise State Public Radio (Samantha Wright, 14 Jan 2015); Wikipedia 'Beaver drop'; Smithsonian Magazine Smart News; National Geographic (Lucy Sherriff, 16 Sep 2021); HeraldNet (Post Register, Rob Thornberry, 19 Dec 2014); East Idaho News (Idaho Statesman, Nicole Blanchard, 18 Dec 2023); Smithsonian Air & Space 'Beavers On Parachutes' (quoting Heter's 1950 paper). Every narrated fact and label is on at least two of them. 1948 and Idaho Fish and Game, Elmo Heter: all seven. Beavers clashing with people round McCall and Payette Lake, felling trees and flooding yards with their dams: Wikipedia, National Geographic, BSPR, East Idaho News. Destination Chamberlain Basin: BSPR, Wikipedia, Smithsonian, National Geographic, East Idaho News (an AP story of Sept 1948 quoted by East Idaho News also mentions the Lochsa-Selway area; the label follows the majority). Heter's 'spooky and quarrelsome' about horses and mules: BSPR, National Geographic, HeraldNet, East Idaho News, Air & Space (exact words). War-surplus parachutes: BSPR, Wikipedia, Smithsonian, National Geographic, Air & Space. A box that held together in the air and opened on landing: all seven (details of the fastening differ: elastic bands, rope binding, tension bands; the animation shows a rope binding and hinged halves, as National Geographic and Wikipedia describe). Geronimo, an old male, dropped again and again on a landing field: BSPR, National Geographic, HeraldNet, Air & Space, East Idaho News. He crawled back into his box ready to go again: Heter's words quoted by BSPR, National Geographic, HeraldNet and Air & Space; East Idaho News quotes a 1948 Statesman column ('actually crawled back in the box'). 76 dropped, 75 survived: all seven. Geronimo among the first, with three young females: National Geographic ('priority reservation on the first ship'), Smithsonian ('one of the first'), BSPR, HeraldNet, Air & Space. August 1948 (first drop 14 August): Wikipedia, National Geographic, East Idaho News; Air & Space speaks of the 1948 fall season, so the narration says 'That year' for the 76 and only the first landing carries the AUGUST 1948 label. A year later dams, lodges ('houses') and colonies on the way: Heter's 1949 observations quoted by HeraldNet and Wikipedia; Air & Space says each group had settled when checked the next season; Geronimo's colony 'very well established' (Air & Space) and 'soon created a colony' (BSPR). Not used: the cost figures ($30 for four beavers vs $7 a beaver, unreconciled), the drop height (500 to 800 ft, one Wikipedia sentence disagrees), the plane type (Beechcraft twin; drawn as a generic unmarked twin), the 2015 rediscovery of the film. The one beaver that died climbed out of its box in the air and fell (National Geographic, Air & Space, HeraldNet, Wikipedia): it is not shown; the narration says 75 landed safely and Rook takes his hat off. Staging liberties, all illustrative: the beaver in the opening box is drawn as Geronimo (he flew among the first); a beaver's nose shows at a breathing hole (the real holes were about an inch across); the corral, the field crew and people's looks are invented; Rook is fictional.

experiments.E1_E2: spine v2: Rook is already on the falling box in shot 4 and doubts it in one line of 1.5 s ('A flying beaver? Please.') with the drop still in frame; no office. The story runs forward from the drop to the landing, then steps back once (why the beavers were moved, the mules, the parachutes, Geronimo's tests) because that is where the comedy and the re-hook are, and returns forward with the flights. Place, date and names are labels (CHAMBERLAIN BASIN, IDAHO; AUGUST 1948; McCALL, PAYETTE LAKE; ELMO HETER, FISH AND GAME; TEST PILOT: GERONIMO).
experiments.E3: The batch brief's Shorts are all made, so this Short is outside it. It opens on the subject close (the box under its canopy with the nose at the hole), the canopy snapping taut 0.15 s in.
experiments.E8: tail 0.4 s; the last line ('Because in Idaho, in nineteen forty-eight,') runs into the first ('a beaver in a wooden box is falling out of a plane...'); the last shot swings back into the opening framing and the canopy luffs back to the half-open state of the first frame.

sound_plan.first_frame: Near-silence under the hook title, a whoosh, then a 'hit' at 0.15 s as the canopy snaps taut and the box jolts (the gate needs an impact in the first second; here it is the story's own sound), and a flap.
sound_plan.music: The engine's score follows the segment moods: hook, tense for Rook's line, action for the landing, calm for the town, tense for the mules, action for the parachutes, wonder for Geronimo's tests, tense for the re-hook, action for the flights, calm for the hush, triumph for the payoff, end.
sound_plan.effects: One to four cues a shot, each tied to something visible: wind in the air, a hit and clunk on landing, a pop and clunk as the box springs open, scratching for gnawing, a creak and crash for the tree, splashes in the flood and the pond, clunks and hits for the bucking mule, ticks for Rook's beak taps, scratches for the tally, a gasp as the box opens in his face, whooshes for each canopy, a caw for Rook's laugh.
sound_plan.hush: Shot 25 (Rook takes his hat off among the open boxes at dusk): the music drops out for 'Seventy-five of them landed safely.'
sound_plan.voice: Narration is ducked over the bed by the engine; measured in the local rehearsal, not listened to.

checklist.A_story: done: score 84/100 with curiosity 10, story 8, payoff 8; facts checked against seven pages; spine v2; shown_moments lists every narrated moment
checklist.B_storyboard: done: every shot has action, expression, camera and sound cue; Rook's mannerisms are hat brim low (4, 18), hat jumping off (7, 15, 20), beak tap (13), feather shed (23), caw-laugh (28), hat off for the hush (25) and pocketing the shiny parachute ring (29); detective actions are the magnifier on the box's knot (15) and the tally of drops (18); no neutral poses under action lines
checklist.B2_retention: done: hook_text set; the first frame is the box under its canopy, close, with the nose at the hole; re-hook at 57% (he climbs back in); one hush (shot 25); tail 0.4 s with a matched loop
checklist.C_previews: done: one still per shot over three sheet rounds, every shot at k=0.2 and 0.8, both ends of every added camera move, and five stills at 720x1280 with production samples; no blown-out or crushed frame where the story has to be seen; faces read at 270x480; Rook on-model
checklist.D_render: engine defaults untouched (60 fps, 720x1280, 16 jobs in the workflow); local rehearsals used 12 fps, 360x640, 6 samples for review only
checklist.E_sound: voice am_fenrir; hook near-silent, music by mood map; every impact cue tied to something visible; voice 16.4 dB over the bed; loudness -14.6 LUFS, peak -1.2 dBFS; loudness range not measured
checklist.F_captions: done: labels fit the frame at rest; no inserts; on-screen dates, names and figures checked against sources
checklist.G_final: three rehearsals; the last reviewed as a 4 fps sheet of the whole video plus full-resolution stills; local gate PASS on rehearsal 3; the full-resolution render and the real gate run in the workflow

quality_gate.method: One run, six review rounds. Round 1: low-res contact sheet of all 30 shots: the basin's mountains rose to about 1 km and walled off the sun and sky, and the town shots were placed with set-local coordinates so they were filmed inside the basin; both fixed. Round 2: sheet again: Heter facing away while unpacking the chute, Rook's face lost under his hat on the dam, Rook standing on top of the flood water with no beaver in frame, the beavers too big for the box (a scale that was never applied), the hush too dark; all fixed. Round 3: every shot previewed at k=0.2 and 0.8: closer cameras on the landing and the bucking mule, the swimming beaver was under the pond surface. Round 4: first rehearsal (12 fps, 360x640): local gate FAIL on nine static stretches; per-shot motion measured, a real camera orbit and push added to 21 weak shots; ends of each move previewed (the hold camera left the fuselage, the notepad covered Rook's face: fixed). Round 5: second rehearsal: two static stretches left (the plane-wide and the ending); the plane shot given a larger move, the sign-off a move, and the loop shot now swings back into the opening framing while the canopy luffs to the first frame's half-open state. Round 6: third rehearsal (changed shots re-rendered): local gate PASS: 30 shots, mean 1.52 s, longest 2.26 s, Rook acting in 12 of 30 shots (40%), -14.6 LUFS, peak -1.2 dBFS, voice 16.4 dB over the bed, closest match to any earlier episode 0.83 (shot 24 against r022-bakari; the limit is 0.93). Reviewed as a 4 fps sheet of the whole video; afterwards the hold shot's camera was kept inside the fuselage for its first quarter-second (a dolly replaces the push), which only adds movement. Duration about 45.5 s. The cloud render runs the real gate at 720x1280 and 60 fps.
quality_gate.not_met: Loudness range was not measured locally; the soundtrack was measured, not listened to.

review.weakest: Humans and the mule are block figures with simple faces; the bucking mule reads more stiff than wild. The beaver's nose shows through a breathing hole drawn larger than the real one-inch holes. In the cargo-door shot Rook is seen mostly from the side and behind. The hush is at dusk and Rook is small in it. Narration and sound were measured, not heard.
